full_title: SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION, PETITIONER, VS. 1ACCOUNTANTS PARTY-LIST, INC., REPRESENTED BY ITS PRESIDENT, CHRISTIAN JAY D. LIM, CHRISTIAN JAY D. LIM IN HIS CAPACITY AS CPA, FROILAN G. AMPIL, ALLAN M. BASARTE, VIRGILIO F. AGUNOD, AND JONAS P. MASCARIÑAS, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Political and Public International Law
syllabus_topic: X. Administrative Law > C. Powers of Administrative Agencies > 1. Quasi-legislative or Rulemaking Power > b. Requisites for Validity
topics: SEC accreditation of external auditors held ultra vires (later reversed)
Accreditation as an additional licensing requirement (Airlift Asia)
A MOA cannot validate a violation of law
Effect of reversal on second motion for reconsideration

other_subjects.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VI. Special Commercial Laws > A. Securities Regulation (RA 8799)

doctrine:
**Caution: this Decision was reversed.** The SEC filed a second motion for reconsideration. In its Resolution of January 28, 2025, the Court En Banc granted it, reversed and set aside this Decision, and declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 of the SRC IRR and SEC MC No. 13-2009 valid and not unconstitutional. The holding below is the 2022 ruling, which the Court has since abandoned. For the controlling rule, see *SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List (Resolution)*, G.R. No. 246027, January 28, 2025.

In 2022 the Court held that **the SEC had no authority to require accreditation of CPAs acting as external auditors of corporations that issue registered securities and hold secondary licenses. It declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 of the Amended IRR of the Securities Regulation Code (R.A. No. 8799) and SEC Memorandum Circular No. 13-2009 null and void.** The SEC's powers under SRC Sec. 5(a) and Sec. 141 of the Corporation Code cover juridical entities such as corporations. Its other SRC powers must be read together with Sec. 5(a); they flow from its jurisdiction over corporations and do not reach individual CPAs or the practice of accountancy. Applying *Airlift Asia Customs Brokerage v. CA*, the Court held that the accreditation was an additional licensing requirement. It curtailed the practice of a profession whose supervision R.A. No. 9298 (Secs. 9 and 31) gives to the Professional Regulatory Board of Accountancy.

The Decision also applied two general rules: (1) ***delegata potestas non potest delegari***: the Board cannot redelegate to another body a power that Congress delegated to it; and (2) **a private agreement, such as a MOA, cannot validate a violation of law** (Civil Code, Art. 1306). The 2025 Resolution did not abandon these rules. It held instead that the MOA delegated nothing, because SEC accreditation regulates the activity of statutory audit, not the profession.
facts:
Respondents were 1Accountants Party-List, Inc. and five CPAs. The organization is a non-stock, non-profit sectoral organization registered with the SEC. It was represented by its President, Christian Jay D. Lim, who also sued in his personal capacity as a CPA. The other CPAs were Froilan G. Ampil, Allan M. Basarte, Virgilio F. Agunod and Jonas P. Mascariñas. They filed a Petition for Declaratory Relief with prayer for preliminary injunction and TRO against the SEC before the RTC of Davao City, Branch 15 (Civil Case No. R-DVO-15-02294-SC). They challenged Rule 68, paragraph 3 of the Amended IRR of the SRC, SEC Memorandum Circular No. 13-2009, and similar circulars. Since 2002, these issuances had required SEC accreditation of CPAs acting as external auditors of corporations issuing registered securities and possessing secondary licenses.

MC No. 13-2009 made the following rules:
- Only an SEC-accredited external auditor (and auditing firm) may be engaged by covered corporations for the statutory audit of their financial statements (Sec. 4.1).
- Applicants pay accreditation filing fees, e.g., P5,000, P3,000 and P2,000 for individual auditors in Groups A, B, and C or D.
- Auditing firms and external auditors who take an engagement without accreditation pay a scale of fines (Sec. 12.4), and so do companies that engage unaccredited auditors.
- An accreditation may be suspended or delisted (Sec. 12.6).

Respondents argued that the issuances were ultra vires, contravened R.A. No. 9298 (Philippine Accountancy Act of 2004), and restricted the right of CPAs to practice their profession. They added that MC No. 13-2009 violated due process and equal protection. The SEC relied on SRC Sec. 5(a), (d), (f), (g) and (n) and Sec. 68, and on Sec. 141 of the Corporation Code. It also invoked a MOA with the BSP, the Insurance Commission and the Board of Accountancy, its police power, and the four-pronged test of reasonable classification.

On March 20, 2018, the RTC declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 and SEC MC No. 13-2009 null and void for being contrary to R.A. No. 9298, unconstitutional, and ultra vires. In an Order dated February 20, 2019, it denied the SEC's motion for reconsideration. The SEC then filed a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45.
issues: Whether the SRC and the Corporation Code authorize the SEC to require accreditation of CPAs acting as external auditors of covered corporations.

Whether the accreditation requirement is an additional licensing requirement that contravenes R.A. No. 9298, which entrusts the regulation of the accounting profession to the Professional Regulatory Board of Accountancy.
Whether the MOA invoked by the SEC can serve as authority for the assailed issuances.
ruling:
The Court said the case presented only one principal issue: whether the RTC correctly declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 and SEC MC No. 13-2009 null and void. It answered yes, on the following grounds.

**1. No, the SRC and the Corporation Code do not authorize the SEC to regulate individual CPAs.** SRC Sec. 5(a) gives the SEC jurisdiction and supervision over "corporations, partnerships or associations." Sec. 141 of the Corporation Code requires "every corporation" to submit an annual report with financial statements certified by an independent CPA. The Court applied the plain-meaning rule (*quoties in verbis nulla est ambiguitas, ibi nulla expositio contra verba fienda est*). Under it, these provisions apply only to juridical entities and nowhere extend to individuals, "moreso CPAs." The other SRC provisions the SEC cited must be read together with Sec. 5(a), because a statute is construed as a whole. All of those powers flow from the SEC's jurisdiction over corporations. In the Court's words, "While petitioner may regulate corporations as well as the securities market, such regulation does not extend to an authority to restrict, even in the slightest degree, the practice of accountancy."

**2. Yes, the accreditation is an additional licensing requirement that contravenes R.A. No. 9298.** *Airlift Asia* defined a license as a "permission to do a particular thing, to exercise a certain privilege or to carry on a particular business or to pursue a certain occupation." A CPA who wants to do a statutory audit of a covered corporation must get SEC accreditation on top of the CPA license, although such audit is already part of the practice of accountancy. The scale of fines in Sec. 12.4 shows the burden. Under Secs. 9(b), (g), (h) and 31 of R.A. No. 9298, the power to supervise the accounting profession and to regulate CPAs is exclusively delegated to the Professional Regulatory Board of Accountancy. MC No. 13-2009's penal clauses contravene that delegation: the fines under Sec. 12.4 and the suspension or delisting under Sec. 12.6. The SEC argued that nothing stopped CPAs from applying for accreditation. The Court answered that "the accreditation itself is the barrier, however flimsy, which prevents the practice of external auditing of covered entities."

**3. No, the MOA cannot authorize the issuances.** Under *delegata potestas non potest delegari*, the Board cannot redelegate to another body a power that Congress delegated to it. Moreover, "a private agreement such as the MOA cannot operate to validate a transgression of a provision of law" (citing Civil Code, Art. 1306). The MOA was therefore void and could not serve as the SEC's authority for the assailed issuances.
disposition:
The petition for review on certiorari was DENIED. The Court AFFIRMED the RTC Decision dated March 20, 2018 in Civil Case No. R-DVO-15-02294-SC. It declared Paragraph 3, Rule 68 of the IRR of the SRC and SEC MC No. 13-2009 null and void. Lazaro-Javier, J. wrote a concurrence, and the other participating Justices concurred.

This disposition was later REVERSED and SET ASIDE by the Court En Banc's Resolution of January 28, 2025, which declared the same issuances valid and not unconstitutional.

bar_questions.q: In 2023, Gemma, a CPA, was told by her lawyer that she did not need SEC accreditation to audit listed companies. The lawyer cited SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List (G.R. No. 246027, June 21, 2022), which declared null and void Rule 68, paragraph 3 of the SRC IRR and SEC MC No. 13-2009. In 2026, Gemma is still unaccredited. She accepts an engagement for the statutory audit of the annual financial statements of a corporation with registered securities and a secondary license. When the SEC questions the engagement, she invokes the 2022 Decision. Is the 2022 Decision still a valid basis for her position?

alac.answer: No. The 2022 Decision has been reversed and set aside. The SEC accreditation requirement is now valid.
alac.legal_basis: In SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List (G.R. No. 246027, June 21, 2022), the Court En Banc declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 of the SRC IRR and SEC MC No. 13-2009 null and void. It reasoned that the SEC's powers under SRC Sec. 5 and Sec. 141 of the Corporation Code cover only juridical entities, and that R.A. No. 9298 entrusts regulation of the accounting profession to the Board of Accountancy. On the SEC's second motion for reconsideration, however, the Court in its Resolution of January 28, 2025 in the same case reversed and set aside the June 21, 2022 Decision and the June 27, 2023 Resolution. It declared the same issuances valid and not unconstitutional. The Court relied on SRC Secs. 5.1(d), 5.1(n) and 72 and on R.A. No. 11232 (Revised Corporation Code) Secs. 177 and 179.
alac.application: Gemma relies on a ruling that no longer stands. The Decision she cites was set aside on reconsideration by the same Court En Banc in the same case. The final word in G.R. No. 246027 is the 2025 Resolution. Under it, the SEC may require CPAs who perform the statutory audit of covered entities to be SEC-accredited. Gemma's engagement is a statutory audit of a covered entity, so the accreditation requirement applies to her.
alac.conclusion: Gemma cannot rely on the 2022 Decision, because the Court reversed it in 2025 and upheld the SEC accreditation requirement.

bar_questions.q: The Commissioner of Customs issued an order that PRC-licensed customs brokers must first be accredited by the Bureau of Customs before they may practice before it. The order imposes accreditation fees and fines for practicing without accreditation. Most of a customs broker's work is done before the Bureau. The Customs Brokers Act of 2004 (R.A. No. 9280) gives a professional regulatory board power over the profession. It also provides that those who pass the licensure examination may practice in any collection district "without the need of securing another license from the BOC." The Commissioner relies only on his general power to issue rules to enforce the customs laws. Is the order valid?

alac.answer: No. The order is invalid because it imposes an additional licensing requirement that the law proscribes.
alac.legal_basis: In Airlift Asia Customs Brokerage v. Court of Appeals, which the Court applied in SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List (G.R. No. 246027, June 21, 2022), the Court defined a license as a "permission to do a particular thing, to exercise a certain privilege or to carry on a particular business or to pursue a certain occupation." It held that a BOC accreditation requirement for customs brokers was a licensing requirement proscribed by law that curtailed their practice. The Court reversed the 2022 Decision in its Resolution of January 28, 2025, but it distinguished Airlift Asia rather than abandoning it. In Airlift Asia, (1) R.A. No. 9280 expressly allows licensed brokers to practice "without the need of securing another license from the BOC"; (2) the Commissioner's mandate to enforce tariff laws does not include power to regulate the profession; and (3) a large part of a customs broker's work is practice before the BOC.
alac.application: The Commissioner's order has all the features that made the CAO in Airlift Asia invalid. A licensed broker cannot practice before the Bureau, where most of the broker's work is done, without first getting the Bureau's accreditation. That makes the accreditation a second license. It directly contradicts the statute's express command that no other license from the BOC is needed. The Commissioner's general power to enforce customs laws is not a power to regulate the customs broker profession, which the law gave to a professional regulatory board. This case is unlike the SEC accreditation upheld in 2025, where no statute expressly barred another accreditation and the rule covered only the statutory audit of a small class of entities.
alac.conclusion: The order is void as an additional licensing requirement contrary to R.A. No. 9280.

bar_questions.q: A statute vests in a professional regulatory board the power to register practitioners of a profession and to promulgate rules on registration requirements, fees, and penalties. To "save on costs," the board signs a Memorandum of Agreement with a government agency, the National Business Office (NBO). Under the MOA, the NBO will issue and renew certificates of registration, set registration fees, and penalize unregistered practitioners. A practitioner fined by the NBO argues that the MOA is void. The NBO answers that the board consented to the arrangement. Who is correct?

alac.answer: The practitioner is correct. The MOA is void and cannot give the NBO power to register or penalize practitioners.
alac.legal_basis: Under the maxim delegata potestas non potest delegari, a power that Congress has delegated cannot be further delegated by the original delegate to another. In addition, a private agreement such as a MOA cannot validate a violation of a provision of law (Civil Code, Art. 1306). (SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List, G.R. No. 246027, June 21, 2022.) In its Resolution of January 28, 2025, the Court reversed that Decision but restated the same maxim. It upheld the SEC's MOA with the Board of Accountancy only because the Board had not delegated its power to regulate the profession: SEC accreditation covers only the activity of statutory audit, and the collaboration did not contravene any statute.
alac.application: Registration of practitioners and the fees and penalties for violating registration requirements are the very powers the statute entrusted to the board. In the MOA, the board does not merely coordinate with the NBO. It hands those powers over to the NBO. This is a redelegation of delegated power, which the board cannot make. The board's consent cannot cure the defect, because a contract cannot authorize what the law does not allow. The arrangement is unlike the SEC-Board MOA upheld in 2025, where the Board kept its full power over the profession.
alac.conclusion: The MOA is void, so the NBO has no authority to fine the practitioner.

notes: REVERSED ON RECONSIDERATION. See SEC v. 1Accountants Party-List (Resolution), G.R. No. 246027, January 28, 2025 (case id gr-246027-20250128). In that Resolution, the Court En Banc granted the SEC's second motion for reconsideration (leave was granted on January 30, 2024). It reversed and set aside this Decision and the June 27, 2023 Resolution, which had denied the first motion for reconsideration with finality, and declared Rule 68, paragraph 3 and SEC MC No. 13-2009 valid and not unconstitutional. The doctrine of this Decision on the SEC's lack of authority is therefore no longer controlling. The bar questions above test only the current rule and points that survived the reversal. The June 27, 2023 Resolution is known only from the 2025 Resolution's recital and is not in the index. The 2022 Decision did not separately rule on the due process, equal protection, or police power arguments. Lazaro-Javier, J.'s concurrence was not used for the doctrine.

superseded_by.label: Reversed
superseded_by.summary: Reversed on the SEC's second motion for reconsideration by the En Banc Resolution of January 28, 2025, which upheld SRC Rule 68, par. 3 and SEC MC No. 13-2009. Study the 2025 Resolution for the controlling rule.
